analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing workers and consumers into private arbitration before disputes arise.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 103 House members, never left the House Judiciary Committee and never got a vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most employment contracts and terms of service today include a clause requiring you to take any dispute to a private arbitrator instead of court, and often waiving your right to join a class action. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable for workplace, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes. You could still choose arbitration after a dispute actually happens — but companies could not require it in advance, and no one could be forced to give up the right to sue together as a group.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with arbitration clauses in their job contracts (including independent contractors), consumers with arbitration clauses in credit card, phone, banking, and online service agreements, and people with civil rights or discrimination claims. All of them would regain the right to have disputes decided by a judge in a public courtroom, and the right to join class actions where many small claims can be combined into one case worth bringing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers with arbitration clauses

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that no pre-dispute arbitration agreement or pre-dispute class-action waiver is valid or enforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, or civil rights disputes [S2] [S3].
It covers independent contractors as well as employees, so gig workers and other misclassified workers are protected too [S3].
It restores the right to participate in class and collective actions, which matters because individual claims are often too small for anyone to sue over on their own [S2] [S3].
A court, not an arbitrator, decides whether the law applies — closing a common move where companies delegate the question to the arbitrator they chose [S3].
Arbitration remains allowed when both sides voluntarily agree after a dispute has already arisen [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that currently use mandatory arbitration clauses — employers, banks, credit card issuers, telecom and online platforms, securities firms, and other consumer-facing businesses — would lose a private, confidential, low-appeal forum they currently control, and would face class action exposure they have largely eliminated. Arbitration providers would lose a large block of business.

drawbacks.text: Court cases are slower and more expensive than arbitration for a single worker or consumer; removing mandatory arbitration could mean some individual claims become harder to resolve quickly [S3] (the bill keeps voluntary post-dispute arbitration for exactly this reason).

Defenders of arbitration argue class actions primarily benefit plaintiffs' attorneys and raise prices for consumers, and that private forums let companies resolve complaints faster; the bill would shift millions of disputes back into the public court system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — restoring access to court and to class actions for tens of millions of people whose contracts currently funnel disputes into a private system that firms control — is substantial and falls on the people least able to protect themselves. The costs are real but modest: some disputes that arbitration resolved cheaply will be slower in court, and businesses bear litigation risk they have avoided. On balance the bill strongly favors workers and consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never held a vote on it, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on April 27, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S5].
That referral was the last action ever taken; no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
It had 102 cosponsors in addition to the sponsor, all Democrats [S4].
A nearly identical bill had passed the House in an earlier Congress, but in this one the House never voted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use mandatory arbitration clauses — large employers, banks, telecom and online platforms, securities firms — keep the current system intact: disputes stay in private arbitration, class actions stay blocked, and nothing changes for them.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers in employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes.

for.name: 102 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including senior Judiciary members; the bill attracted no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with sole jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred to the committee in April 2023, the committee never took the bill up — no markup or vote was ever scheduled, so it could not reach the floor.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with the bill bottled up in committee, no vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Business coalitions have long opposed federal limits on mandatory arbitration, arguing it is faster and cheaper than litigation; they did not need to act here because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 102 cosponsors, plus the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding the House majority the bill never got a vote [S4].

industries.industry: Large employers with mandatory arbitration policies
industries.note: Mandatory arbitration clauses let employers resolve discrimination, wage, and firing claims in a private forum with limited appeal and no class action. The bill would strip that advantage, so their interest runs directly against workers' access to court.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, telecom and online platforms
industries.note: Consumer contracts and terms of service routinely force disputes into arbitration and block class actions. The bill would end both practices for consumer disputes.
The bill defines consumer disputes to include purchases of securities and investments, removing forced arbitration for retail investors.
The bill covers workers regardless of whether they are classified as employees or independent contractors, closing the route platforms use to keep contractor disputes out of court.
Firms that administer mandatory arbitration cases would lose a large block of business, though voluntary post-dispute arbitration remains legal.
